13	> \[

20	## 1. Every such map has at least three fixed points
21

24	\omega(aA+bB)=4\pi(a+b),\qquad

45	## 2. A smooth function on \(M\) with exactly three critical points
46	
47	Start with
48	\[
49	f_0(x,y)=x_3+y_3.
50	\]
51	It has four critical points: its minimum, its maximum, and the two saddle points
52	\[
53	(e_3,-e_3),\qquad (-e_3,e_3).
54	\]
55	
56	We will collapse a zero-level arc connecting the saddle points. The collapse is not a diffeomorphism at the collapsed point, so smoothness there must be proved.
57	
58	### 2.1 Coordinates containing the arc
59	
60	Define stereographic coordinates
61	\[
62	\sigma(p,q)=
63	\frac{(1-p^2-q^2,\;2q,\;2p)}{1+p^2+q^2}
64	\]
65	and the chart
66	\[
67	\kappa(t,d,v,w)
68	=\bigl(\sigma(t+d,v),-\sigma(t-d,w)\bigr).
69	\]
70	Its image is the complement of one point in each sphere, so it is an open subset \(U\subset M\) diffeomorphic to \(\mathbb R^4\).
71	
72	In these coordinates,
73	\[
74	g(t,d,v,w):=f_0(\kappa(t,d,v,w))
75	=
76	\frac{2(t+d)}{1+(t+d)^2+v^2}
77	-
78	\frac{2(t-d)}{1+(t-d)^2+w^2}.
79	\]
80	The four critical points have coordinates
81	\[
82	(\pm1,0,0,0),\qquad (0,\pm1,0,0).
83	\]
84	The first pair are the saddles; the second pair are the maximum and minimum.
85	
86	Crucially,
87	\[
88	g(t,0,0,0)=0\qquad\text{for every }t.
89	\]
90	Thus the segment
91	\[
92	I=[-1,1]\times\{0\}^3
93	\]
94	lies in the zero level and connects the two saddles.
95	
96	### 2.2 An explicit diffeomorphism removing the segment
97	
98	For \(r>0\), put
99	\[
100	A(r)=
101	\begin{cases}
102	r+\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{r}{1-r/2}\right),&0<r<2,\\[6pt]
103	r,&r\ge2.
104	\end{cases}
105	\]
106	It extends smoothly to \(r=0\), with \(A(0)=1\), and is smooth at \(r=2\), because
107	\[
108	\exp\!\left(-\frac{r}{1-r/2}\right)
109	=e^2\exp\!\left(-\frac4{2-r}\right).
110	\]
111	
112	Also \(A'(r)>0\). Indeed, for \(0<r<2\), setting \(z=r/(2-r)>0\) gives
113	\[
114	A'(r)=1-(1+z)^2e^{-2z}>0,
115	\]
116	since \(e^z>1+z\).
117	
118	For \(\theta=(\theta_1,\theta')\in S^3\), define
119	\[
120	G(r\theta)=\bigl(A(r)\theta_1,\;r\theta'\bigr).
121	\]
122	Then
123	\[
124	G:\mathbb R^4\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4\setminus I
125	\]
126	is a diffeomorphism.
127	
128	Here are details of that assertion. Its radius-\(r\) images are the ellipsoids
129	\[
130	\frac{q_1^2}{A(r)^2}+\frac{|q'|^2}{r^2}=1.
131	\]
132	Both axes increase strictly. For any \(q\notin I\), the left side decreases strictly from a value greater than \(1\) to \(0\), so precisely one such ellipsoid contains \(q\). The implicit-function theorem gives a smooth inverse. Equivalently, its Jacobian determinant is
133	\[
134	\det DG(r\theta)
135	=
136	A'(r)\theta_1^2+\frac{A(r)}r(1-\theta_1^2)>0.
137	\]
138	Finally, \(G\) is the identity for \(r\ge2\).
139	
140	### 2.3 Flattening at the collapsed point
141	
142	The pullback \(g\circ G\) need not be smooth at the origin. We fix that by flattening its radial variable.
143	
144	For \(s>0\), define
145	\[
146	\chi(s)=
147	\begin{cases}
148	\exp\!\left(-\dfrac{s}{1-s}\right),&s<1,\\
149	0,&s\ge1,
150	\end{cases}
151	\qquad
152	h(s)=s\exp\!\left(-\frac{\chi(s)}{s^2}\right).
153	\]
154	The function \(h\) is smooth and strictly increasing on \((0,\infty)\), equals \(s\) for \(s\ge1\), and extends to a function flat at \(0\).
155	
156	For strict increase, observe that \(\chi'\le0\), and
157	\[
158	h'(s)=
159	\exp\!\left(-\frac{\chi(s)}{s^2}\right)
160	\left(1-\frac{\chi'(s)}s+\frac{2\chi(s)}{s^2}\right)>0.
161	\]
162	For flatness, \(\chi\) is smooth near \(0\) and \(\chi(0)=1\), so \(h\) and all its derivatives decay faster than every positive power of \(s\).
163

167	=
168	\bigl(A(h(s))\theta_1,\;h(s)\theta'\bigr).

173	\mathbb R^4\setminus I,
174	\]
175	and is the identity outside the radius-\(2\) ball.
176	
177	Define \(F:M\to\mathbb R\) by
178	\[
179	F(\kappa(z))=
180	\begin{cases}
181	g(\Psi(z)),&z\ne0,\\

195	B(0,\theta)=g(\theta_1,0,0,0)=0.
196	\]

203	F(\kappa(s\theta))=h(s)C(h(s),\theta).
204	\]

206	
207	Thus \(F\in C^\infty(M)\).

209	### 2.4 Counting its critical points
210	
211	Away from \(z=0\), \(\Psi\) is a diffeomorphism. Consequently,
212	\[
213	d(g\circ\Psi)(z)=0
214	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
215	dg(\Psi(z))=0.
216	\]
217	The two saddle points \((\pm1,0,0,0)\) are omitted from the image of \(\Psi\). The other two critical points, \((0,\pm1,0,0)\), remain. They are unchanged because \(h(1)=1\) and their first coordinate is zero.
218	
219	The origin is a critical point because the new function is flat there.
220	
221	Hence
222	\[
223	\operatorname{Crit}(F)
224	=
225	\left\{
226	(e_3,e_3),\;
227	(-e_3,-e_3),\;
228	(e_1,-e_1)
229	\right\}.
230	\]
231	In particular,
232	\[
233	\#\operatorname{Crit}(F)=3.
234	\]

236	## 3. Scaling excludes nonconstant one-periodic trajectories
237	
238	It remains to justify that a sufficiently small autonomous Hamiltonian \(\varepsilon F\) has no additional time-one fixed points arising from nonconstant periodic trajectories.
239	
240	Regard \(M\subset\mathbb R^6\), and write \(V=X_F\). Since \(V\) is smooth and \(M\) is compact, it has a finite extrinsic Lipschitz constant \(L\):
241	\[
242	|V(p)-V(q)|\le L|p-q|,\qquad p,q\in M.
243	\]
244	Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with
245	\[
246	\varepsilon L<2\pi,
247	\]
248	and let \(H_t=\varepsilon F\).
249	
250	Suppose \(\gamma\) is a one-periodic trajectory. Put
251	\[
252	E=\int_0^1|\dot\gamma(t)|^2\,dt.
253	\]
254	Since \(\dot\gamma=\varepsilon V(\gamma)\) and
255	\(\int_0^1V(\gamma(t))\,dt=0\), the variance identity gives
256	\[
257	\begin{aligned}
258	E
259	&=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}
260	  \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1
261	  |V(\gamma(t))-V(\gamma(s))|^2\,dt\,ds\\
262	&\le
263	\frac{\varepsilon^2L^2}{2}
264	  \int_0^1\!\!\int_0^1
265	  |\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|^2\,dt\,ds\\
266	&=\varepsilon^2L^2
267	  \int_0^1|\gamma(t)-\bar\gamma|^2\,dt\\
268	&\le \frac{\varepsilon^2L^2}{4\pi^2}E.
269	\end{aligned}
270	\]
271	The last step is the ordinary periodic Wirtinger inequality in \(\mathbb R^6\).
272	
273	Our choice of \(\varepsilon\) forces \(E=0\). Thus every one-periodic trajectory is constant, and
274	\[
275	\operatorname{Fix}(\varphi_{\varepsilon F}^1)
276	=\operatorname{Crit}(F).
277	\]
278	There are exactly three such points.
279	
280	At the collapsed point, all derivatives of \(F\) vanish. In particular,
281	\[
282	D\varphi_{\varepsilon F}^1(e_1,-e_1)=I.
283	\]
284	This is precisely where allowing degenerate fixed points matters.
285
